You call Python's built-in print function with two arguments: the string 'Maximum value:' and the variable max_num. The comma between arguments makes print insert a space between them, and print adds a newline at the end. print will also convert the numeric value to text for you.

You must ensure max_num is defined before this line runs; if it isn't you'll get a NameError. Also avoid trying to join the string and number with + without converting the number to a string first (that causes a TypeError). Don't confuse the argument-separating comma here with creating a tuple—inside print it separates arguments.

As a best practice, make the output clear and consistent. You can use an f-string for cleaner formatting, e.g. print(f'Maximum value: {max_num}'), which avoids manual conversions. If you want different spacing or no newline, control it with the sep and end parameters of print.

distractors.description: You might pick >= because you think it handles the case when the first and second numbers are equal, and that using >= somehow 'fixes' tie situations. That is a common intuition: using >= feels more inclusive and therefore safer. If you use this line, the program will usually still return one of the correct maximum values, but it changes how ties are resolved. For example, when the first and second inputs are equal and also equal to the third, the nested checks will end up selecting the third value instead of the first or second. In short, the condition is looser than intended for the control flow here — it treats equality the same as strictly greater, which changes which branch you take in tie cases. This differs from the intended comparison because it does not strictly require the first number to be greater than the second before proceeding; that subtle change can alter which value is chosen when values are equal. That is why this line is a plausible but incorrect choice for replacing the original comparison.

You might choose this because you confuse the positions of the second and third inputs and think checking num1 against num3 first is fine. If you use this line, the program no longer checks whether the first number is greater than the second before entering the first branch. That leads to incorrect results when the second number is actually larger than the first but the first is larger than the third. For example, with inputs num1=6, num2=9, num3=5, this condition is true (6 > 5) so the code goes into the branch that ultimately may set the maximum to num1, even though num2 is the true maximum. In short, this distractor compares the wrong pair of variables and breaks the intended decision flow, so it is not a correct replacement.

You may pick this because you confuse the inequality direction or accidentally write the opposite sign. If you use this line, the test selects the branch for when the first number is less than the second, which is the opposite condition of what the decision needs at that point. That inversion flips the program's control flow: cases where the first number is actually the largest will be sent to the other branch, and the code will favor the second or third number incorrectly. For instance, with num1=10, num2=7, num3=3 the condition is false, so the code will go into the else-branch and may choose a non-maximum value. This distractor thus implements the wrong comparison direction and will cause incorrect maximum selection in many cases.
